title: Vocal nodules and voice problems
intro: Vocal nodules are small, benign calluses on the vocal cords caused by repeated strain, common in singers, teachers and others who use their voice a lot. They cause hoarseness, a breathy or tired voice and vocal fatigue. Voice therapy is the main treatment, and surgery is rarely needed.

sections.heading: How the voice works
paragraphs: Sound is made when air from the lungs makes the two vocal cords vibrate. They must close fully and vibrate evenly. When cords are overworked, the contact points can thicken and form nodules, which stop them from closing properly and cause a rough or airy sound. Polyps and cysts can cause similar symptoms.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: Hoarseness, a breathy or weak voice, voice that tires quickly, a lower pitch, difficulty reaching high notes and throat discomfort. Symptoms often worsen through the day with use. Persistent hoarseness lasting more than three to four weeks should be checked by a doctor, as other causes, including cancer, need to be excluded, especially in smokers.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: An ear, nose and throat specialist looks at the vocal cords with a small flexible camera, or a rigid scope, often with a strobe light to show how they vibrate. A voice therapist assesses voice use. The aim is to identify the type of lesion and contributing habits such as shouting, talking over noise, throat clearing, smoking and reflux.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Voice therapy with a speech and language therapist teaches efficient voice use, breathing, relaxation, and healthy habits. Most nodules shrink or disappear with therapy over weeks to months. Treat reflux, stop smoking, stay hydrated and avoid whispering and throat clearing. Surgery under general anaesthesia is considered only if therapy fails, followed by voice rest and therapy.

sections.heading: Looking after your voice
paragraphs: Drink water, rest the voice during illness, use amplification in noisy settings, avoid straining, warm up before long use and ensure adequate sleep. Professionals who use their voices can have training from vocal coaches. Seek help early rather than pushing through hoarseness.

examples.title: Protecting the teaching voice
examples.text: Imagine you teach all day and end up hoarse. You could use a microphone, take silent breaks, drink water and ask about voice therapy.

examples.title: Noticing persistent hoarseness
examples.text: Suppose you have been hoarse for six weeks. You might see a doctor for a vocal cord examination rather than waiting.
